title: The “shitty choices” tweet that won’t die
summary:
The most brutal line that keeps getting re-used like a Swiss Army knife: @visakanv’s “people don't wanna make better choices, they wanna make shitty choices and then complain about the shitty outcomes.” It starts as a throwaway quote in his “best one-liners” list (Feb 2020), and then becomes this weird little boundary object everyone keeps stapling onto new situations—therapy, dating, procrastination, online discourse, even AI safety.

The arc is basically: Visa builds the philosophical runway in 2018 (“people avoid decisions so they can avoid being responsible”), then in early 2020 the quote gets “discovered” and deployed. @nosilverv points it at academics whining about cancellation (“just start shitposting online and build an antifragile brand”), @imhinesmi self-dunks with the classic “how do i get better at socializing / try talking to people / …anything else?” and @GeniesLoki adds the sharp mechanism: solutions are “rude” because they remove plausible deniability—people want “you to validate their cope.” That triggers pushback from @xsphi, who basically says “this is a laziness narrative and laziness isn’t a root cause,” and Visa’s response is: tone is doing a lot of work; the observation can read as hostile OR as “clarity of someone who faces reality heroically.”

Then it mutates from a complaint about complainers into a whole agency/responsibility framework. Visa ties it to “Thingification” (people begging for a neat magic concept), “word magic” (stop asking the universe for stuff you don’t actually want), and power (“people pay lip service to empowerment but don’t want the responsibility”). The peak “escape velocity” moment is @goblinodds in 2024: learned helplessness dissolves into “there’s no skill here it’s just deciding,” plus the darker add-on that non-deciders will blame whoever decides but also can’t do anything about it because doing anything requires… deciding. By 2025, @DefenderOfBasic tries to reduce the whole mess to “fear,” and @reimao42 pops in with the Dostoyevsky-esque counter that sometimes people choose self-harm just to assert free will.

Why care: it’s basically a diagnostic for when someone (or you) is secretly optimizing for blame-avoidance, sympathy, or identity-preservation instead of results. And it also explains why “helpful advice” so often starts fights—because solving the problem threatens the story that made the problem socially useful.
